comments.author: Hiten Shah
comments.text:
Hey Product Hunt, Hiten here.

My setup has gotten a little weird. I've got Macs running agents and local models, with work continuing even when nobody's sitting in front of them.

Sometimes I just want to check a Terminal, open a browser, or use an app on one of those machines. Getting there usually means opening Screen Sharing and navigating a whole second desktop.

Sam and I have been working on Beam to make this easier.

With Beam, you pick a window on another Mac and it opens alongside the apps on the Mac you're using. It gets its own Dock icon and a place in ⌘Tab. You can type into it and resize it like a normal window. You can also move files between Macs and hear the app's audio. The app itself keeps running on its original machine.

When one window isn't enough, Beam lets you open an entire screen or the whole Mac.

I'm especially excited about using Beam with headless Mac minis and Studios. They can keep running agents and other work while I use their apps from whichever Mac I'm sitting in front of.

Beam works on Apple silicon Macs running Sonoma or later. You can connect over your local network or through Tailscale, with encrypted connections directly between Macs.

It's available now and free to try for 20 minutes every day. Download it at Beam.win.

A few weeks ago I asked people on X to show me their weird multi-Mac setups. The thread got over 100 replies, and I've loved seeing what everyone has built.

One thing I've become fascinated by is the Mac nobody sits in front of.

If you have one, what do you still need to open Screen Sharing for?

Hi everyone!  
  
Figma actually used Specs to build Specs. One of its engineers documented edge cases, embedded FigJam diagrams, and handed the spec and his teammates' comments to a coding agent. As development progressed, he used MCP to keep the original doc updated.  
  
Now you can drop a .md file onto the Figma canvas, embed actual frames or FigJam diagrams, and pull them back out to edit. Teammates and Figma's agent can work through comments together. Send the spec link to Codex via Figma MCP, and it gets the Markdown and the linked design context.  
  
Of course Figma found a way to make .md files draggable!

Hi Product Hunt 👋 I’m Sançar, co-founder of readywhen.  

If you're a founder, you probably feel like if you stop, everything stops.

  
Most founders don’t run their day from a desk. They run it from the car, the school gate, the walk between meetings. That’s where the promises get made. A quote on a call. A “leave it with me” at the door. A reply you’ll send “when I’m back”. By the time you’re back, half of them have slipped, and the rest are still in your head at 11pm.  

You started your business because you’re brilliant at something, not to chase follow-ups from memory. So we put readywhen where you already are.  

readywhen is the senior personal assistant for owner-led businesses, and today it’s on WhatsApp. It has its own phone number, its own computer, and a project board that keeps track of everything on your plate. Call it. Message it. Voice-note it. And it gets real work done.  

A few things to send it today:

  
💬 “Find three options for our team offsite and pencil the best one into my calendar”  
💬 “Turn these notes into a client proposal and have it ready for me to check”  
💬 “What am I subscribed to, and what can I cancel?”  
💬 “Go through my inbox and tell me what actually needs me today”

  
It works with the tools you already use (1000+ of them), and nothing sends without your OK.  

It’s free during the limited beta: Join the WhatsApp beta  

The team and I are here all day. Tell us the first thing you’d hand readywhen, what’s missing, and what you’d want it to do next. I’ll read every comment.  

See you on WhatsApp 👋

Sançar  
Co-founder, readywhen

Hey Product Hunt 👋  
  
I'm Isabella, co-founder of Gleap. Our team builds AI-native customer support for fellow software teams, and today we're launching the newest member of our AI team: Kai Resolve.  
  
Why we built it

Kai Support already takes care of the easy cases, quickly and with a low token cost. But some tickets need more than a good answer: someone has to dig into the data to really help the customer. That's where Kai Resolve comes in. It looks into the ticket, finds bugs and hands them to your team with a much better handover. It also picks up the context of the conversation, and through MCP it can add feature requests that come up in a chat straight to your roadmap. So one agent sorts it all out: inquiries, feature requests and bugs.

What Kai Resolve does

🔍 looks at the screen recording, console and network logs and the click trail that came with the report

🧑‍💻 checks account data and your code, read-only, in a sandbox, and points to the exact file and line

✅ answers the customer, flags a likely bug for your team with the cause and the evidence, or adds the feature request to your roadmap

Based on our Gleap data, Kai Resolve resolves 75% of all tickets automatically. And when it isn't sure, it says so and asks your team instead of guessing.

Who it's for

Software teams whose tricky tickets wait for a developer: support leads, developers on support duty, product managers and founders.

Pricing

About $0.49 per investigation on average, billed for the work it does. Included from the Team plan, with a 7-day free trial and no credit card.

🎁 Launch-day deal for the Product Hunt community: sign up today and get 50% off for one year with the code KaiResolve26.

What we'd love from you

Try it on a real ticket from your own queue and tell us where it got it right and where it didn't. Tough tasks are very welcome. Lukas will share more about the technical side right below, and the whole team is here all day to chat.

A big thank you to Thomas Schranz for hunting us, and to all of you for stopping by 🙏  
See you in the comments below 👋

Hey @shivam_kushwaha16,  
  
Florian here, CTO at Gleap. I'm jumping in since this one is technical 🙂  

For multi-step bugs, Kai Resolve doesn't have to guess the steps. It reads what came with the report: the screen recording, the click trail, and the console and network logs. That lets it follow what the user actually did, step by step. It then compares that with the account data and reads your code, read-only, to find where things go wrong. Bugs like "change setting A, open page B, save C, and it breaks" usually work well, because the evidence shows the whole path.  

How deep it can go mostly depends on what it can see. If you connect more sources through MCP, like your monitoring, it can also trace issues that never show up on the user's screen, like an error spike or a slow backend call. And when something is still unclear, it doesn't guess. It hands the ticket to your team with what it checked, what it found, and what's still open, so the developer doesn't start from zero.  

If you have a nasty multi-step bug in your queue, give it a try and let me know how it did. I'm happy to look at the result with you 🙌

Hey Product Hunt 👋 Tobi here, co-founder of Gleap.

We’ve been building support tools for years, and one thing kept bugging me: the hardest part of support was never writing the reply. It was figuring out what actually went wrong. AI got really good at answering questions, but most “AI support” stops right there. We wanted something that does the part that actually hurts: the investigation.

That’s Kai Resolve. It looks into every ticket like an experienced teammate would, answers what it can, and hands the rest to your team with the cause and the evidence ready. And the more context you give it (your docs, your code, your past tickets), the more it solves on its own.

For me, this is the support tool I always wished we had.

I’d love to hear from everyone running support: what’s the part of the digging that takes your team the longest? 🙌

comments.author: Lukas Böhler
comments.text:
Hey Product Hunt 👋

Lukas here, co-founder of Gleap.

I’ve been building software for most of my life, and the part I always hated was the gap. A customer reports a bug, it becomes a ticket, the ticket becomes a Jira issue, and weeks later someone ships a fix. The customer who reported it never finds out. The feedback loop just… never closes.

That’s why I’m so excited about Kai Resolve. It’s the first time support and engineering feel like one team.

Here’s what happens when a hard ticket comes in:

🔍 Kai Resolve investigates it like a developer would: logs, click trail, session replay, and the actual code in your GitHub repos  
✅ It tells your team what’s going on (bug, feature request or setup issue) and lists the files it read, so you can check its work  
🛠️ For a real bug, it prepares a coding task. One click hands it to Kai Code, Claude Code, Codex or Cursor, and you get a pull request to review

  
💬 Once the fix is live, the customer hears back on the same ticket they opened - automatically.

What I love most is that last step. The person who took the time to report the problem actually hears “we fixed it, thank you.” I think that’s what turns users into fans.

Your engineers stay in control the whole way: they review every PR and decide what ships. Kai Resolve just takes on the digging and the back-and-forth that used to eat our week. We run our own support on it every day, and it’s honestly changed how we build Gleap.

I’d love your feedback, especially from devs and founders: how does the loop from customer report to shipped fix work on your team today?

I’ll be here all day 🙌

평생 소프트웨어를 만들어 오면서 제가 늘 싫어했던 것은 '단절(gap)'이었습니다. 고객이 버그를 제보하면 티켓이 되고, 티켓이 Jira 이슈가 되고, 몇 주 뒤에 누군가 수정본을 배포합니다. 정작 문제를 제보한 고객은 그 사실을 전혀 알지 못하죠. 피드백 루프가 결코 닫히지 않는 겁니다.

그래서 저는 Kai Resolve에 큰 기대를 걸고 있습니다. 고객 지원과 엔지니어링이 처음으로 하나의 팀처럼 느껴지게 해주기 때문입니다.

까다로운 티켓이 들어오면 다음과 같이 작동합니다:

🔍 Kai Resolve가 개발자처럼 조사합니다: 로그, 클릭 경로, 세션 리플레이, 그리고 GitHub 저장소의 실제 코드를 살핍니다.
✅ 팀에 상황(버그, 기능 요청 또는 설정 문제)을 설명하고 읽은 파일 목록을 함께 제시하므로 조사 결과를 쉽게 검증할 수 있습니다.
🛠️ 실제 버그인 경우 코딩 작업을 준비합니다. 클릭 한 번이면 Kai Code, Claude Code, Codex 또는 Cursor로 전달되어 검토할 수 있는 PR(Pull Request)이 생성됩니다.

💬 수정 사항이 배포되면 고객이 처음 열었던 바로 그 티켓을 통해 자동으로 완료 안내를 받게 됩니다.

제가 가장 좋아하는 부분은 바로 마지막 단계입니다. 시간을 내어 문제를 제보해 준 사람이 실제로 "수정되었습니다, 감사합니다"라는 답을 듣게 되는 것이죠. 저는 그것이 사용자를 팬으로 만든다고 생각합니다.

엔지니어는 모든 과정에서 통제권을 유지하며 모든 PR을 직접 검토하고 배포 여부를 결정합니다. Kai Resolve는 그저 일주일을 잡아먹곤 하던 원인 조사와 번거로운 커뮤니케이션을 대신 맡아줄 뿐입니다. 저희도 매일 자체 고객 지원에 이를 사용하고 있으며, Gleap을 만드는 방식 자체가 완전히 바뀌었습니다.

특히 개발자와 창업자분들의 피드백을 듣고 싶습니다. 현재 여러분의 팀에서는 고객 제보부터 수정 배포까지의 루프가 어떻게 돌아가고 있나요?

오늘 하루 종일 이곳에 있겠습니다 🙌

comments.author: Florian
comments.text:
Hey Product Hunt 👋 Florian here, CTO at @Gleap .  

@isabella_salzmann covered the why, so here's the part I'm most excited about as an engineer: how Kai Resolve investigates.  

When a tricky ticket comes in, it works like a good developer would: → follows the click trail and watches the session replay → reads the console and network logs to see what actually failed → checks the account data for anything unusual → reads your code and points to the exact file and line  

The more it can see, the deeper it goes. Connect your monitoring or internal tools via MCP, and it can trace issues that never show up on the user's screen.  

Send it the bug your team has been avoiding for weeks, and tell me how it did. I'm here all day for any questions about how it works under the hood 🔍

comments.author: Sezer İltekin
comments.text: Hi Product Hunt! I'm Sezer, the maker of walkai-talkai. I wanted to talk to my AI coding agent without sitting at the keyboard, so I wired it to a handheld radio. Press PTT, say what you want ("run the tests and fix any failures"), and the agent gets it. When it's done, the answer comes back through the radio as a short spoken summary. How it works: • The radio connects to your Mac with a standard audio cable (K-plug or 3.5 mm); the radio's VOX handles transmit. • Speech is transcribed on your Mac with Whisper. Your radio audio is never uploaded. • The command is typed into Cursor, Claude Code or Antigravity, or sent straight to OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, DeepSeek or Ollama in API Mode. • The reply is spoken back with on-device neural voice, with VOX tones and a roger beep, in English or Turkish. Honest notes: it's macOS only (Apple Silicon, macOS 13+). Anything you transmit can be heard by others on that frequency, and someone on the channel could even speak commands to your agent, so have your agent ask for confirmation before irreversible actions. Radio licensing rules are your responsibility. It's a one-time lifetime license (no subscription) with a 14-day refund. I'd love to know: what would you say to your agent over the radio?
